title: The Buyer Type You Attract Decides the Price You Get
linkedin:
Most owners talk about their business as if it has one true value. It doesn't.

A trade buyer, a private equity fund and your own management team will rarely price the same business the same way, even looking at identical financials.

A trade buyer often isn't just buying your profit line. They're buying a customer base, a team, or market access they'd otherwise spend years building. That's synergy value, and it sits on top of the standalone numbers, but only if the seller makes the strategic case explicit.

A financial buyer is underwriting a return over three to five years. They price off predictable, recurring cash flow and discount hard for exactly what a growth story often hides: thin margins, customer concentration, an owner who is still the first call for every major client.

A management buyout is usually the quietest exit available, and for the right business it protects culture in a way an external sale can't. It also tends to settle lower, mostly because the buying team is financing it personally rather than drawing on outside capital.

The mistake we see most often is preparing the business generically, then discovering mid conversation which buyer actually showed up, and that the number in the owner's head was built for someone else entirely.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

facebook:
Quick thought for anyone who's ever wondered what their business is actually worth. The honest answer is: it depends who's asking.

A competitor might pay more than the numbers suggest, because they're buying your customer base or your team, not just your profit. A private equity buyer prices off predictable cash flow and won't pay for a growth story built on thin margins. And selling to your own management team usually means a lower price, simply because of how they'd have to finance it.

Most owners never think about which of these they're actually likely to attract until an offer lands. Have you ever sat down and worked out which type of buyer your business would suit best?

A question worth sitting with if you're an owner-led business anywhere on the East Coast, even years out from selling: who do you actually expect to buy your business one day, and have you prepared for that specific buyer?

It matters more than most owners realise. A competitor buying for strategic reasons, a private equity fund buying for a return, and your own management team buying to keep things running are rarely looking at the same business the same way, even when the financial statements are identical. A trade buyer can pay a premium for the customer base or market access they'd otherwise spend years building. A financial buyer prices off certainty and predictable cash flow, and discounts hard for owner dependence. A management buyout tends to settle lower, largely because of how it gets financed.

The businesses that end up negotiating from a position of strength are usually the ones that worked out early which buyer they were realistically preparing for, rather than discovering it partway through a conversation. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
